chapter: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
title: The tiny Hotcha, Billie's inimitable style and singing table to table
summary: The Hotcha held five or six tables; nobody can copy Billie; singers in Chicago and New York worked tables for tips, and in Chicago sang softly so the next table had to pay.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: Do you remember singing from table to table?
-- was just a little joint. Yeah, the Hotcha was a little tiny place.
Just about like that. Yeah. It had about four or five tables, or maybe five or six tables, that's all. Just a little narrow place.
That's all. But I think Billie made a lot of money in there, because people was crazy about her.
She was just so unusual. Billie Holiday was an unusual singer. She had a style that nobody will ever copy.

Nobody will ever be able to copy Billie Holiday, I don't care who they are. If they're going to try to do songs that Billie Holiday did, they should do them in their own way, but not try to copy Billie Holiday, because they'll never do it.
I guess I'm asking if she was moving from table to table, but I guess if it was that small she couldn't move much.
Well, she'd sing a song and if somebody else would ask her to sing something she'd go and sing for them.
But usually, when you'd go in and you'd get her to the table you wouldn't let her go.
But people -- singers were doing the same thing in New York as at Chicago. In other words, going --
Just going from table to table.
-- from table to table and collecting --
Yeah, but you know, in Chicago we were slick. We'd sing really softly, like Joe Oliver and them would
So nobody could hear, and if you wanted to hear it at the next table you'd pay for it.
